summary.text: 道 means “road” or “way,” and also “method” or “principle.” Its received analysis joins 辵, associated with travel, and 𩠐 (首), treated as a sound component; their proposed historical sound resemblance is less apparent in modern Mandarin dào and shǒu.

formation.text: The received analysis is phonosemantic: 辵 contributes a travel-related meaning, while 𩠐, corresponding to 首, supplies a sound cue. The Shuowen account calls the formation ideographic; Duan Yucai’s commentary also identifies 首 as phonetic.

components.text: 辶 is the conventional side form of 辵, which contributes a travel-related category in 道. This side/full-form relationship does not itself imply a historical sequence.

The received analysis identifies 𩠐, corresponding to 首, as the sound component. In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese, 首 *l̥uʔ and 道’s “way” reading *[kə.l]ˤuʔ share a similar final sound; modern Mandarin shǒu and dào differ. This comparison supports, but does not independently prove, the component analysis.

sound_limitation.text: The reconstructions provide a sound comparison but do not by themselves establish that 首 is the component in the ancient graph or prove its phonetic role.

sound.text: In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese, 首 *l̥uʔ and 道’s “way” reading *[kə.l]ˤuʔ share a similar final sound, unlike their modern Mandarin readings.

history.text: 道 is reported in bronze inscriptions. The bronze-style and Shuowen seal-style images are modern redrawings that illustrate reported forms; they do not establish a direct sequence or confirm the bronze graph’s parts.
The received dictionary analysis gives 辵 plus 𩠐. Shuowen also records 𡬹, written with 首 and 寸, as an older-text form, but its relationship to 道 is unresolved.
A proposed interpretation of the bronze form as a head carried in a ritual is disputed and lacks direct support. Proposed derivation from 導 and cognacy with Proto-Hmong-Mien are also unverified.

uncertainties.text: The earliest individual inscription and its date remain unresolved. The reported 行, 止, and 亍 parts, and their proposed merger into 辵, are not confirmed by an inspected inscription.
The relation of 𡬹 to 道 is unresolved. A proposed derivation from 導 and proposed Proto-Hmong-Mien cognacy lack verified word-history evidence.

senses.text: 道 is defined as a way people travel, and a transmitted poem uses it in a road context. “Road; way” is the earliest meaning supported here, though the poem’s composition date and the graph’s first attestation remain unresolved.
Dictionary entries also record “route” and “journey.” Their listing does not establish when these uses arose or how they relate to the road sense.
道 is used for a method or principle, including philosophical Dao. The available examples do not date these senses or establish how they developed from “road; way.”
Dictionary entries record guiding and speaking uses, but do not establish their chronology or relationship to the road and method senses.

limitations.text: The poem’s road-context use does not establish its composition date or the graph’s earliest attestation. Dictionary sense lists and examples do not provide a dated sequence for later meanings.
The proposed derivation from 導 is unverified; neither a borrowing direction nor semantic development from 導 is established.

items.period: Bronze-script style; Commons file does not specify a period. Dong Chinese separately labels its displayed bronze example Early Western Zhou, circa 1000 BCE, but this particular Commons glyph should not inherit that date.
items.tradition: Bronze inscription style; modern digital vector redraw
items.caption: This bronze-script-style rendering of 道 has a complex central form with strokes extending to either side. Bronze forms are reported for the character, but this redraw does not identify a specific inscription or establish the parts’ historical interpretation.
items.alt: Black bronze-script-style 道 glyph with a dense central form and strokes extending to the left and right, on a white field.
items.selection_reason: Its distinctive graphic form helps illustrate the reported bronze-script evidence, while the caption avoids treating the redraw as an artifact or asserting an unverified component analysis.
items.rights: Wikimedia Commons description declares the SVG public domain, including a public-domain release of the rendering.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style, conventionally associated with the Han Shuowen tradition; SVG upload in 2006 does not date the glyph itself.
items.tradition: Small-seal script style; modern Inkscape vector redraw
items.caption: This Shuowen seal-script-style rendering corresponds to the dictionary’s analysis of 道 as 辵 plus 𩠐 (首). That account describes the character as a way people travel and also records “one-way access” as a definition.
items.alt: Black seal-script-style 道 glyph with a tall, rounded central form and enclosing strokes, on a white field.
items.selection_reason: It provides a useful comparison with the bronze-style rendering and illustrates the received Shuowen analysis, without implying that the two images establish a direct chronological sequence.
items.rights: Wikimedia Commons description declares the SVG public domain, including a public-domain release of the rendering.

limitations.text: Both images are modern digital redrawings, not photographs or facsimiles of identified ancient artifacts. No specific bronze inscription, date, or earliest attestation is established here; the report that 道 first appears in bronze inscriptions remains unverified at the level of an individual object.

The bronze form’s graphic parts and their proposed relation to 行, 止, and 辵 are not confirmed by an inspected inscription. Shuowen’s 辵-plus-𩠐 analysis is a historical dictionary account, not independent proof of the bronze form’s morphology.
